title: How to Set Up Gooten Shipping Regions Before You Launch
excerpt: Shipping settings decide whether your delivery promise is honest. This guide maps production locations to the regions you sell into, then turns that map into promises you can keep.
body: Most delivery complaints blamed on the carrier are actually configuration problems. In print on demand fulfilment, transit time is only half of the promise; the other half is production, and production happens wherever the item is made. If your best selling hoodie is produced in one region and your customer is on another continent, no carrier choice will rescue a three day promise. Before you write a single delivery estimate on a product page, you need a map that connects each product to where it is made and how long it takes to reach each market you sell into.

Start with demand rather than geography. Pull last quarter of orders and list your destination markets by share, then keep only the markets that account for roughly ninety percent of volume. Everything else goes into a rest of world bucket with a conservative estimate. For each of those markets, take your top ten SKUs and record the production location and the typical transit window. You will usually find two or three distinct patterns hiding in that table, and those patterns become your shipping zones.

Turn the patterns into a simple zone table with three rows. For each zone, write down production days, transit days, and a buffer you add on top. The buffer is not padding for its own sake; it absorbs the weekend order that sits until Monday and the occasional remake after a print defect. Most stores land on two to four production days and a buffer of one to two days for domestic zones, with a noticeably wider buffer for cross border zones where customs handling is out of anyone's control.

Now convert the table into storefront language. Replace the single global promise on your product pages with a per zone estimate that updates once the customer enters a destination, and repeat the same window in the cart and the confirmation email. A promise that changes by region is slightly more work to maintain, but it removes the gap between what the customer expects and what actually arrives. The DTCwise Fulfillment & Shipping category at /category/fulfillment keeps the current shortlist of fulfilment tools with ratings and pricing for exactly this kind of decision.

Write the exception rules at the same time. Remote destinations inside an otherwise fast zone deserve their own line in the table. Peak season deserves a temporary buffer: from mid November to late December, most production networks run longer, and a promise you set in September will quietly become false. Decide now whether you extend the published estimate or close the affected zones to new orders, because both are better than discovering the problem through a wave of support tickets in December.

Close the loop with measurement. Once a month, compare the promised window against actual delivered dates for a sample of orders in each zone, and adjust the table where you consistently miss. A zone that beats its estimate can be tightened to win more conversions; a zone that misses needs a longer promise before it needs a new carrier. The Gooten listing at /tool/gooten shows current pricing, production coverage and the integration details worth checking before you commit a catalog to it.
